title: The Sun on your plate: where the energy of a food chain goes

summary.text: A cow eats grass all day, yet a kilogram of grass makes far less than a kilogram of cow. So where does the rest go? A food chain carries the Sun's energy from a plant to the animals that eat her, and on to the next eater. But the energy does not stay in any of them. At every step most of it leaves as heat, and only a small part is left to feed the next eater. In this unit you burn a peanut to see how much energy a bite holds, build three kinds of pyramid, follow a dead leaf through a hidden chain, and ask what a living body really is.
summary.art: A notebook page with the Sun drawn in the top corner, an arrow of light reaching a rice plant, then thinner and thinner arrows to a grasshopper, a frog and a snake, and wavy heat lines rising from every one of them.

intro.hook: Put the back of your hand on your forehead. Feel how warm you are? Where did that warmth come from, and where is it going now?
intro.text: Your body is about as warm as a cup of tea you could sip. Nobody lit a fire inside you. The warmth comes from your last meal, which was a plant or an animal who ate plants, which caught light from the Sun. Now that warmth is leaving your forehead and spreading into the room. In this unit you will follow the Sun's energy along a food chain, and find out what happens to it at every step. You will also meet a chain in the mud that starts with a dead leaf.
intro.art: A child with a hand on their forehead, and faint heat waves rising from the hand and the head into a room, with a plate of rice and dal on the table.

outcomes: I can explain that a food chain is a path for energy that begins with sunlight caught by producers, and name the trophic levels along it.
I can explain where the energy of a meal goes: into new body, into heat made by respiration, and into parts that are not eaten or not digested.
I can draw and read a pyramid of numbers, of biomass and of energy, and explain why the first two can be upside down but the energy pyramid cannot.
I can follow a dead-leaf chain, name detritivores and decomposers, and explain why so much of the energy in forests and mangroves passes through dead matter.
I can explain that atoms go round and round through living things, while energy goes through them once and ends as heat that leaves the Earth.
I can run a fair test, say what I think, what I saw and why, and explain why a measured number is always smaller than the energy that was really there.
I can say what scientists agree on, and what they still argue about: whether plants or hunters run a food web, and whether every food chain starts with sunlight.

terms.meaning: A step in a food chain, counted from the producers. Producers are level 1, the animals that eat them are level 2, and so on.
terms.example: In rice, grasshopper, frog, snake, the frog is at level 3.
terms.art: A staircase of four steps, with a rice plant on the first step, a grasshopper on the second, a frog on the third and a snake on the fourth.

terms.meaning: A living being who makes her own food from light, or from chemicals, instead of eating other living things.
terms.example: A rice plant makes sugar from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.
terms.art: A green rice plant with sunlight arrows hitting the leaves and sugar drawn inside.

terms.meaning: An animal who eats producers. She is at level 2.
terms.example: A cow, a grasshopper, a honeybee drinking nectar and a parrot eating seeds.
terms.art: A cow grazing, a grasshopper on a leaf and a honeybee on a flower, all labelled level 2.

terms.meaning: An animal who eats primary consumers. She is at level 3. One who eats those is a tertiary consumer, at level 4.
terms.example: A frog eating a grasshopper is a secondary consumer. A snake eating the frog is a tertiary consumer.
terms.art: A frog catching a grasshopper, with a snake behind the frog, and level numbers 3 and 4 beside them.

terms.meaning: A hunter at the top of a food chain, whom no other animal hunts when she is grown.
terms.example: A tiger in a forest, or a big shark in the sea.
terms.art: A tiger standing on a rock above a forest, with a small crown-shaped gap above her head to show nobody is higher.

terms.meaning: Dead leaves, dead wood, dung and dead bodies, broken into small pieces.
terms.example: The brown, soft mud under a mangrove tree is mostly detritus.
terms.art: A handful of dark, crumbly leaf mud held in a palm, with tiny leaf pieces and threads of white fungus in it.

terms.meaning: An animal who eats detritus and breaks it into smaller pieces.
terms.example: An earthworm, a millipede, a dung beetle and a mangrove crab.
terms.art: A millipede and an earthworm on a dead leaf, with a dung beetle rolling a ball beside them.

terms.meaning: A fungus or a bacterium who digests dead matter outside her body and soaks up the food. She sends the atoms back into the soil, water and air.
terms.example: The mould that grows on a damp chapati, and the white threads under a fallen log.
terms.art: White fungus threads spreading through a rotting log, with tiny bacteria drawn in a zoom-in circle.

terms.meaning: What every living cell does to free the energy in food. The cell uses food and oxygen, and makes carbon dioxide, water and heat. It is not the same as breathing.
terms.example: A compost heap gets warm because the microbes in it respire.
terms.art: A cell drawn as a round room with a sugar going in, oxygen going in, and carbon dioxide, water and red heat waves coming out.

terms.meaning: The mass of living matter, often counted after the water has been dried out.
terms.example: All the grass on a football field weighs far more than all the grasshoppers on it.
terms.art: A big sack labelled grass beside a tiny pouch labelled grasshoppers on a pair of balance scales.

terms.meaning: A drawing with one bar for each trophic level, where the width of the bar shows how many living beings are at that level.
terms.example: One banyan tree can feed thousands of insects, so its pyramid of numbers is not a pyramid.
terms.art: A spindle-shaped drawing with a thin line for one tree at the bottom, a wide bar for insects above it, and narrow bars for birds and a hawk.

terms.meaning: A drawing with one bar for each trophic level, where the width of the bar shows how much energy flows through that level in a year.
terms.example: If grass takes in 1000 units of energy, the grasshoppers who eat her pass on about 100 and the frogs about 10.
terms.art: A tall pyramid of four bars, widest at the bottom, with energy numbers 1000, 100, 10 and 1 written in the bars.

terms.meaning: All the food chains of a place joined together, because most animals eat more than one kind of food.
terms.example: A crow eats grain, fruit, insects and scraps, so the crow sits in many chains at once.
terms.art: A tangle of arrows between a rice plant, a mango tree, a grasshopper, a crow, a frog and a snake.

terms.meaning: Energy stored in the way atoms are joined together. Sugar, starch and fat hold a lot of it.
terms.example: A peanut holds chemical energy, which comes out as heat and light when it burns.
terms.art: A peanut drawn as a box with a small spring-like bond picture inside, and a flame and heat waves coming from the peanut.

terms.meaning: Making food from chemicals instead of from sunlight. Some bacteria do this.
terms.example: Bacteria near hot deep-sea vents use a smelly gas, hydrogen sulfide, to make food for tube worms.
terms.art: A tall white and red tube worm beside a black smoky vent on the dark sea floor, with tiny bacteria drawn in a zoom-in circle.

terms.meaning: The one-way journey of energy through living things, from the Sun, through the food chain, and out as heat.
terms.example: Sunlight on a leaf, then a caterpillar, then a bird, with heat leaving at each step.
terms.art: A long arrow starting at the Sun, passing through a leaf, a caterpillar and a bird, with small red heat arrows leaving each one.

explanations.concept: Trophic levels: counting the steps from the Sun
explanations.definition: A trophic level is a step in a food chain. Producers are level 1, animals who eat producers are level 2, animals who eat those are level 3, and so on.
explanations.description: The word trophic comes from a Greek word for food. Producers are plants, algae and some bacteria who make their own food. Everyone else is a consumer, and a consumer is counted by how many steps she is from the producers. An arrow in a food chain points from the eaten to the eater, because it shows which way the energy goes. Most food chains have only three to five levels. Decomposers are not on one level. They feed on the dead bodies and wastes from every level. A food chain is a simple picture, and real places are tangled into webs, but the counting is still useful.
examples: Rice plant (level 1), grasshopper (level 2), frog (level 3), snake (level 4).
In a pond: tiny algae (level 1), water fleas (level 2), small fish (level 3), kingfisher (level 4).
In the sea off Kerala: tiny algae (level 1), sardines or mathi (level 2 or 3), tuna (level 4).
explanations.art: A staircase going up from a rice plant to a snake, with the level number on each step and an arrow from each step to the next.

explanations.concept: How little of the Sun a plant catches
explanations.definition: Photosynthesis changes light energy into chemical energy stored in sugars. Over a whole season, a green field stores only about 1 part in 100 of the sunlight that falls on it, or less.
explanations.description: Sunlight falls on a leaf. Some light bounces off, some passes through, and some warms the leaf and the water inside her. A small part is used to join carbon dioxide and water into sugar. That sugar holds chemical energy, which means energy stored in the way atoms are joined. Even sugarcane, one of the best crop plants, stores only a few parts in 100. A forest or the open sea stores less. So the first step of every food chain already starts with a small share of the Sun. All the animals on Earth are fed by that small share.
examples: A rice field in Thanjavur gets sunlight all day, and the rice grains and straw hold only a small share of it.
Sugarcane stores more sunlight than most crops, which is why sugar mills can run on the cane left over after the juice is pressed.
Coal is plant energy stored for about 300 million years. When coal burns, it gives back sunlight that fell on forests long before dinosaurs.
explanations.art: Sunlight arrows falling on a rice field, with most arrows bouncing away or turning into heat, and only a few thin arrows ending in grains of rice.

explanations.concept: Three exits: where the energy of a meal goes
explanations.definition: When an animal eats, the energy of the food goes three ways: some is not taken in, some is used up by respiration and leaves as heat, and a small part becomes new body.
explanations.description: Think of a grasshopper eating a leaf. First, she does not eat all of the plant, and she does not digest everything she does eat. The dung she leaves behind still holds energy, and decomposers will eat it. Second, her cells use most of the food she took in to move, to keep working and to repair themselves. That is respiration, and it ends as heat. Third, a small part is built into her body as growth, and into eggs. Only this third part, and her body when she dies, is left for the next eater. This is why a hunter at the top of a chain gets only a small part of what the plants first caught.
examples: A cow does not eat the roots of the grass, and she leaves dung. Dung beetles roll it into balls and eat it.
A tiger leaves the bones, the skin and the stomach contents of a deer. Vultures, hyenas, beetles and fungi finish them.
A child grows only a little each month. Most of the food she eats goes to run her body and to keep her warm.
explanations.art: A grasshopper on a leaf with three arrows leaving her: a pile of dung, red heat waves, and a thin arrow into a small egg.

explanations.concept: Respiration: why every living body gives off heat
explanations.definition: Respiration is how cells free the energy in food. A cell uses food and oxygen and makes carbon dioxide, water and heat.
explanations.description: Breathing and respiration are different. Breathing brings oxygen into your body. Respiration happens in every cell, and uses that oxygen to break down sugar and release its energy. Some of that energy is used to move, to build and to send signals. The rest becomes heat, and no cell can turn heat back into food. Plants respire too, day and night, and so do fungi and bacteria. That is why a compost heap can get hot enough to steam, why a crowded bus is warm, and why a bee colony keeps its nursery warm in winter. Where there is life, there is a little heat leaving.
examples: A pile of fresh grass cuttings or a compost heap can reach 50 degrees or more, because microbes respire.
Your body stays near 37 degrees by making heat from food, all day and all night.
A crowd of children in a small room warms the room, because each child is making heat.
explanations.art: A cell as a round room, with sugar and oxygen coming in on the left, and carbon dioxide, water and red heat waves going out on the right.

explanations.concept: Why 'about a tenth', and why it changes
explanations.definition: About one tenth of the energy at one level reaches the next level. The real number is anywhere from less than 2 to more than 30 out of 100, depending on who is eating.
explanations.description: In 1942 Raymond Lindeman measured how much energy passed from one level to the next in a lake in Minnesota. In his lake it was around a tenth to a fifth. Later work showed the number is not a law. Warm-blooded animals, such as birds and mammals, spend most of their food on staying warm, so they turn only a few parts in 100 of their food into new body. Cold-blooded animals such as insects and fish keep their body temperature close to their surroundings, so they turn much more of their food into body. A chain through insects and fish can therefore pass up more energy than a chain through birds and mammals. About a tenth is a handy guess, and no more.
examples: A hen turns a few parts in 100 of her grain into body. A fish can turn ten times that share.
A lizard can live for weeks on a few insects. A sparrow of the same weight needs food every day to stay warm.
Plankton in the sea pass on a bigger share than a cow does, because plankton are not warm-blooded.
explanations.art: Two food bowls with arrows: a hen with a thin arrow going to a small egg and thick red heat waves, and a fish with a thicker arrow going to a larger body.

explanations.concept: Three pyramids: numbers, biomass and energy
explanations.definition: A pyramid of numbers counts the living beings at each level. A pyramid of biomass weighs them. A pyramid of energy measures how much energy flows through each level in a year.
explanations.description: Each pyramid answers a different question. Numbers ask: how many? Biomass asks: how much living matter is here right now? Energy asks: how much energy passes through this level in a year? In a grass field all three are wide at the bottom and narrow at the top. Energy is the fairest of the three, because one big animal and one tiny animal are compared by the same unit. The energy pyramid is always wide at the bottom, whatever the place, because a level can never pass on more energy than it receives. Numbers and biomass can behave oddly, as the next card shows.
examples: A grass field: 1000 grass plants, 100 grasshoppers, 10 frogs, 1 snake. The numbers shrink at each step.
A pond: the weight of all the water plants is much more than the weight of all the fish.
Any place: the energy bars always shrink upwards, because heat leaves at every step.
explanations.art: Three side-by-side pyramids for the same grass field, labelled numbers, biomass and energy, each drawn from bars of different widths.

explanations.definition: Pyramids of numbers and of biomass can be the wrong way up, but a pyramid of energy never is.
explanations.description: A single banyan tree is one producer, yet thousands of insects and many birds live from her. So the pyramid of numbers is thin at the bottom, wide in the middle and thin at the top. In the open sea, the tiny algae are eaten almost as quickly as they grow. At any one moment their total weight can be smaller than the weight of the tiny animals who eat them. The biomass pyramid is then upside down. Yet the algae divide every day or two, so over a year they make far more food energy than the animals do. The energy pyramid, which counts a whole year, stays the right way up.
examples: One banyan tree, 1000 insects living on her leaves, 20 birds, 1 hawk. The numbers are narrow, wide, narrow, narrow.
One deer can carry thousands of ticks. The ticks are more numerous than the deer.
In many open seas, the weight of tiny animals at one moment is more than the weight of the algae.
explanations.art: Two pyramids side by side: a spindle-shaped banyan numbers pyramid, and an upside-down biomass pyramid for the open sea with tiny algae at the thin bottom.

explanations.concept: Food webs and levels that are not whole numbers
explanations.definition: Most animals eat from more than one level, so an animal's trophic level is the average level of her food plus one, and is often not a whole number.
explanations.description: A crow eats grain and fruit, which are level 1, and also insects, which are level 2. Half her food is level 1 and half is level 2. The average is 1.5, so the crow sits at 2.5. Scientists use this idea to give every animal a number. They also measure it in the body. The nitrogen in an animal's body gets a little heavier at each step up a food chain, and the size of that change tells scientists the level. In 2013 a team estimated that people around the world, on average, are at about 2.2. That is near a pig or an anchovy. Most of what most people eat comes from plants.
examples: A cow eats only grass and straw. She is at level 2.
A rat snake eats half frogs (level 3) and half rats (level 2). She is at 3.5.
A person who eats mostly rice, dal and vegetables, with a little curd, is a little above 2.
explanations.art: A crow in the middle of a web with a number 2.5 above her head, and arrows from grain, fruit and insects joining at her.

explanations.definition: A detritus food chain begins with dead plant matter, not with a living plant being eaten. Detritivores and decomposers feed on it, and other animals feed on them.
explanations.description: Most leaves are never eaten alive. In a forest, grazing animals eat less than a fifth of the leaves. The rest falls, dies and is eaten as detritus. In open water the balance is the other way, and most algae are eaten alive. In a mangrove, fallen leaves are pulled into burrows by crabs. Fungi and bacteria soften the leaf and grow on it, and tiny worms and shrimp-like animals graze on that film. Prawns, fish and herons then feed on those. So a dead leaf is not the end of a food chain. It is the start of another. Scientists are still measuring how much of a mangrove's food comes from its leaves, and how much from algae and plankton.
examples: Mangrove leaf, then crab, then fish, then heron, in a Kerala backwater.
Fallen leaf, then fungus, then springtail, then centipede, in the soil of a plant pot.
Cow dung, then dung beetle, then mynah, then a cat.
explanations.art: A mangrove leaf falling into the mud, with arrows to a crab, a tiny worm, a prawn, a fish and a heron.

explanations.concept: Atoms go round, energy goes through
explanations.definition: The atoms in living things are used again and again. The energy is not. It enters as light or chemical energy and leaves as heat.
explanations.description: A carbon atom can be in the air as carbon dioxide, then in a leaf as sugar, then in a grasshopper, then in a frog, then back in the air when the frog respires. The same atom can go round many times. Energy is different. Sunlight arrives, plants catch a small part, and at every step much of it is turned into heat. That heat spreads out and finally leaves the Earth as invisible infrared light. The Earth sends out almost exactly as much energy as it gets from the Sun, which is why its temperature stays steady. A food chain is a small stretch of this one-way road.
examples: The carbon in a tiger's muscle was in the air as carbon dioxide only weeks or months earlier, before a plant took it in.
A candle flame, a human body and a leaf all give out heat that ends in the sky.
Satellites measure the light the Earth receives and the heat it gives out, and the two nearly match.
explanations.art: A circle of arrows for atoms going round between air, a leaf, a deer and soil, and a straight arrow of energy going from the Sun through them and out to space.

explanations.concept: Who runs a food web: the plants below or the hunters above?
explanations.description: Scientists agree that plants feed everyone and that hunters can change what the grazers do. They disagree about which matters more, and the answer seems to depend on the place. This is one of the biggest open arguments in ecology.
examples: In the Serengeti, more rain means more grass, more wildebeest and more lions.
Where sea otters were hunted, sea urchins ate the kelp forests. When otters returned, the kelp came back.
In a pond, adding fish can change the number of algae, two levels below.
explanations.art: A food web drawn twice. In the first drawing a big arrow goes up from the plants. In the second a big arrow goes down from a hunter.

perspectives.explanation: Energy supply sets the limit. Plants decide how much food there is, so they decide how many grazers and how many hunters can live there. More rain or more nutrients means more of everything.

In 1960 three American ecologists, Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin, argued that the world is green because hunters keep the grazers from eating all the plants. Take away the hunters, and the grazers can strip the land.
Many ecologists today say both are true. Which one is stronger depends on the place. Hunters seem to matter more in lakes and seas, and plants set the limits more on dry land.

explanations.concept: The hidden eaters: parasites, microbes and viruses
explanations.description: Most food-web drawings leave out parasites, microbes and viruses. A parasite is an animal who lives on or in another and feeds from her. In some studies of estuaries, parasites took part in more than half of the feeding links. In the sea, bacteria feed on dissolved food, and viruses burst bacteria and algae open so that their contents return to the water for others. Scientists think this hidden loop carries a very large share of the sea's energy, but they are still working out how much. The tidy chain we draw is a small part of what is really going on.
examples: Ticks and worms on a deer pass energy from the deer to themselves.
A tiny drop of seawater holds a million bacteria and about ten times as many viruses.
A virus that bursts a sea alga lets bacteria feed on the alga's insides.
explanations.art: A zoom-in circle of seawater with bacteria, viruses and a burst alga, beside a normal food chain of algae, tiny animals and fish.

agreed.text: Nearly every food chain on Earth begins with producers who capture energy from sunlight.
agreed.evidence: Satellites measure how much light green plants and algae take in, and scientists measure the oxygen and sugar that photosynthesis makes.

agreed.text: Energy flows one way through a food chain and leaves as heat, while atoms are used again and again.
agreed.evidence: In 1942 Raymond Lindeman measured the energy at each level of a lake and found less at every step. Satellites measure the heat leaving the Earth.

agreed.text: At every step, most of the energy is not passed on. It is used in respiration, left uneaten, or left in dung.
agreed.evidence: Scientists weigh the food an animal eats, her growth and her wastes, and measure the heat she gives off. In most animals the new body is only a small share of the food.

agreed.text: Dead matter is one of the biggest pathways of energy in nature.
agreed.evidence: A 1999 study by Just Cebrian of many places found that in forests grazers eat only a small share of what the plants make, and the rest goes to the dead-leaf chain.

agreed.text: A pyramid of energy is never upside down, but pyramids of numbers and biomass sometimes are.
agreed.evidence: Energy cannot grow on its way up a chain. Counts of banyan insects and weights of sea plankton show upside-down pyramids.

agreed.text: Most animals feed at more than one trophic level.
agreed.evidence: Scientists check this by looking inside stomachs and by measuring nitrogen in bodies. Nitrogen gets a little heavier at each step, as Minagawa and Wada found in 1984.

challenging.claim: The 'one-tenth rule' is a law of nature.
challenging.for: Lindeman's lake in 1942 gave numbers near a tenth for some steps. A round number is easy to remember, and it makes a good first estimate.
challenging.against: Measurements in many animals give anything from under 2 to over 30 parts in 100. Warm-blooded animals pass on much less than cold-blooded ones.

challenging.claim: Eating plants always uses less of the Earth than eating animals.
challenging.who: Many nutrition and climate studies, and many people.
challenging.for: A hen or a pig turns only a small share of her grain into meat, so feeding grain to animals wastes energy that people could eat directly.
challenging.against: Cows, goats and sheep turn grass and straw, which people cannot digest, into milk and meat, often on land where crops will not grow. In India, milk is a key food for many families. Fish and shellfish can be raised on food that people do not eat.

challenging.claim: Decomposers are the end of the food chain, and nothing eats them.
challenging.who: Some older drawings of food chains.
challenging.for: Decomposers come last in the drawing, after everything has died.
challenging.against: Tiny worms called nematodes graze on fungi and bacteria, and springtails eat fungi. Decomposers are food for others, and their atoms and energy move on.

challenging.claim: Every food chain starts with sunlight.
challenging.for: Almost everything on land and in the sea depends on photosynthesis.
challenging.against: In 1977 scientists found animals living around hot vents at the bottom of the sea, in total darkness. In 1981 Colleen Cavanaugh and her colleagues showed that bacteria inside tube worms make food using a smelly gas, hydrogen sulfide, from the vents. Their chain starts with chemical energy from inside the Earth.

challenging.claim: Energy flow is the best way to understand a food web.
challenging.who: Raymond Lindeman, and ecologists who followed him.
challenging.for: Energy gives one unit that lets us compare a mouse, a tiger and a tree. It can be measured, added up and checked.
challenging.against: Some ecologists say that energy counts hide who matters. A small predator who keeps a grazer in check can matter much more than her share of the energy. Disease, space and seasons matter too.

big_questions.q: You eat rice, and the rice was sunlight. Then the energy leaves you as heat. If none of it stays, what exactly is it that you are made of?
big_questions.hint: Think about the atoms that stay and the energy that passes. Which of the two is you?

big_questions.q: A candle flame stays the same shape while the wax burns away. Is a living body more like a thing, or more like a flame?
big_questions.hint: What would have to stop for the flame to go out? What would have to stop for a body to stop being alive?

big_questions.q: An animal's trophic level changes with what she eats. Is a level something an animal has, or something she does?
big_questions.hint: A crow at 2.5 eats more insects one week and more fruit the next. Where is the crow's level then?

big_questions.q: Nine tenths of the energy at every step becomes heat. Is that waste, or is the heat the point?
big_questions.hint: Think about the warmth that keeps you alive, and the heat that keeps the Earth from freezing.

big_questions.q: If the tiger depends on the deer, and the deer on the grass, and the grass on the Sun, is anyone really at the top?
big_questions.hint: Draw arrows for who needs whom, not for who eats whom. What does the picture look like?

big_questions.q: When we choose what to eat, we also choose which beings get fed and which do not. How should we decide?
big_questions.hint: A cow, a field of rice, a fishing boat and a farmer's family are all in the picture.

big_questions.q: Nobody can see energy. How do scientists know it moves from a plant to a grasshopper?
big_questions.hint: Think of measuring heat from burning food, and the weights of what is eaten and what is left.

big_questions.q: Is a mangrove forest one big being, or a crowd of beings who happen to live together?
big_questions.hint: Think about the leaf, the crab, the prawn and the heron, and what each one needs from the others.

story.title: The Leaves in the Net Bag
story.note: A made-up story. The village is imagined, but pokkali fields near Kochi, where rice and prawns are grown in turn in the same flooded fields, are real, and so are Kudumbashree, the women's groups of Kerala. The science in it is real: in mangrove creeks, fallen leaves are eaten by crabs and softened by microbes, and a large share of the food that fish and prawns eat starts from them. Scientists are still measuring how large the share is, and algae and plankton matter too.
text: Every November, after the rice was cut, Anjana's grandmother let the sea into the field. At high tide she opened the wooden gate, and salty water ran in from the canal and covered the stubble. By January the field was full of prawns. Anjana, who was in Class 4, loved the dawn net, when the whole field flashed silver and her grandmother, Muthassi, laughed like a girl.
This January the net came up nearly empty.

Muthassi pulled it in again and again. A few prawns, a few small fish, a lot of mud. By the third morning she did not laugh. She sat on the bund with the empty net across her knees and looked at the water as if it had told her a lie.

Their neighbour, Sebastian Uncle, came along the bund with his bicycle. He looked at the egrets standing in the shallows. 'There is your trouble,' he said. 'Herons and egrets. They are eating all your prawns. Put a net over the field, Muthassi. I will help you.'
Muthassi nodded slowly. But Anjana was counting. She had learned counting from her teacher, who said that if you want to know something, first count it.

She counted the birds on the bund that morning. Two herons and three egrets. She asked Muthassi how many there were last year. 'Oh,' said Muthassi, 'the whole bund was white. Twenty at least. You could not walk without frightening them.'
Anjana frowned. 'Muthassi, if the birds were eating the prawns, there would be more birds this year, not fewer. A bird that eats well stays, and brings her friends. Birds go where the food is.'
Sebastian Uncle scratched his head. 'Then why are the prawns gone?'
'I do not know,' said Anjana. 'But the birds are the last ones in the line. Something happened at the start of the line.'

That evening she asked Muthassi what prawns eat. Muthassi thought. 'The soft mud, my child. The brown mud at the bottom, near the kandal trees. The mud that smells sweet when you turn it.' The kandal were the mangrove trees that grew along the canal bend, with their stilt roots standing in the water like a hundred thin legs.
'And the mud comes from the kandal?'
'I never asked,' said Muthassi. 'It was always there.'

The next morning Anjana walked to the canal bend. Half the kandal trees were gone. Stumps stood in the mud like a row of teeth, and a new wooden landing had been built where the roots used to be. A man had cleared them in the dry months so that boats with tourists could come. Nobody had told Muthassi, because nobody thought it had anything to do with a rice field.

Anjana did not say anything. She picked up an old onion bag from the bank. She filled it with brown, fallen leaves from under the trees that were left. In a second bag she put green leaves, plucked from a branch. She tied both to a bamboo stake in the creek, where the tide would wash through them.
She went back every morning for four days.

On the first day the bags looked the same as when she left them. On the second day the brown leaves were slimy, with a thin brown skin on them. On the third day they were soft and torn at the edges. On the fourth day, when she lifted the bag, tiny pale things were wriggling on the brown leaves. A crab as big as her thumb was pulling a piece of leaf back into the mud.
The green leaves had hardly changed. They were hard and smooth, and nobody had touched them.

She borrowed Muthassi's reading glasses and held one lens over the brown leaf. It was alive. Worms as thin as a hair, and a swarm of creatures like tiny shrimps, were grazing on the soft skin of the leaf. It was like looking into a kitchen full of cooks.
'Muthassi,' she called. 'Come and look.'
Muthassi looked through her own glasses, which she had not known could do that. She was quiet for a long time.

'Nobody eats a green leaf,' said Anjana slowly. 'It has to fall first. It has to die and go soft, and the tiny things grow on it, and the crabs and the small worms eat them. Then the prawns eat the worms and the soft mud. Then the herons eat the prawns. The line does not start with a living plant being eaten. It starts with a leaf that has fallen.'
'And when the man cut the trees . . .' said Muthassi.

'No leaves fell. So no mud was made. No small things. No prawns. And then the herons went away to find a better creek. They did not steal anything, Muthassi. They were following the prawns, and the prawns were following the leaves.'
Sebastian Uncle came to see the net bag. He looked at the brown leaf, then at the stumps, then at his shoes. He did not say a word about herons again.

That month the women of the village, the ones who meet every Thursday in the Kudumbashree group, collected seeds from the kandal trees that were left. The seeds look like long green pencils. They pushed them into the mud at the canal bend, one by one, in a long line. Muthassi said it would take years.
'That is all right,' said Anjana. 'The prawns can wait. They are good at it.'
And she tied a fresh bag to the stake, to see what the new leaves would bring.
story.epiphany: The line of eaters did not start with a living plant. It started with a leaf that had fallen. Cut the trees, and the whole line goes hungry, even the birds at the end.
ask: Anjana did not believe that the herons were eating all the prawns. What fact made her doubt it?
Why did the green leaves stay hard, while the brown leaves turned soft and full of life?
If you wanted to bring the prawns back sooner, what could you do besides planting seeds?
