games.title: Level Detective: how high in the chain is she?
games.context: This is a guessing game. Each card names a living being and what she eats. You guess her trophic level, and then work it out. It shows that a level is an average, and often not a whole number.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a pile with creature names on the front, a pencil and a score sheet beside the pile.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and shuffle them. Print the score sheet.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while the others write a guess on a slip of paper.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone writes a guess.

setup.art: The reader turning the card around, showing the sum on the back, and the guess slips lying face up.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. The closest guess wins.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a creature and her diet on the front, and her level with the working on the back

items.f: Grasshopper. She eats only grass. Guess her level (1 to 5).
items.b: Level 2. Grass is level 1, and she eats only grass. Her level is 1 plus 1.

items.f: Cow. She eats grass and paddy straw, all of it from plants.
items.b: Level 2. Her whole diet is level 1, so she is 1 plus 1.

items.f: Zooplankton, tiny drifting animals of the sea. They eat tiny algae.
items.b: Level 2. Tiny algae are producers at level 1.

items.f: Honeybee. She drinks nectar and eats pollen from flowers.
items.b: Level 2. Nectar and pollen come from plants, which are level 1.

items.f: Earthworm. She eats dead leaves in the soil. Count dead leaves as level 1, the same as the plants they came from.
items.b: Level 2. Dead plant matter keeps the level of the plant.

items.f: Mangrove crab. She pulls fallen mangrove leaves into her burrow and eats them.
items.b: Level 2. Fallen leaves are plant matter at level 1.

items.f: Frog. She eats grasshoppers and caterpillars, who eat only plants.
items.b: Level 3. Her food is all level 2, so she is 2 plus 1.

items.f: Spider. She catches flies and grasshoppers in her web. Both are level 2.
items.b: Level 3. Her food is all level 2, so she is 2 plus 1.

items.f: Tiger. She eats chital deer, who eat only plants.
items.b: Level 3. Deer are level 2, so a tiger who eats only deer is level 3.

items.f: Vulture. She eats dead cattle. Cattle are level 2.
items.b: Level 3. A scavenger takes the level of what she eats, plus one.

items.f: Female mosquito. She drinks the blood of cattle, who are level 2.
items.b: Level 3. Her blood meal comes from a level 2 animal.

items.f: Insect-eating bat. She catches moths and beetles who eat plants.
items.b: Level 3. Moths and beetles are level 2, so she is 2 plus 1.

items.f: Sardine, or mathi. Half of her food is tiny algae and half is zooplankton.
items.b: Level 2.5. The algae are 1 and the zooplankton are 2. The average is 1.5. Add 1.

items.f: Crow. Half of her food is grain and fruit, and half is insects who eat plants.
items.b: Level 2.5. Grain and fruit are 1, insects are 2. The average is 1.5. Add 1.

items.f: Prawn. Half of her food is rotting leaf mud and half is tiny worms who feed on that mud.
items.b: Level 2.5. Leaf mud is 1, the worms are 2. The average is 1.5. Add 1.

items.f: Hen. Three quarters of her food is grain and kitchen scraps, and one quarter is insects.
items.b: Level 2.25. Three quarters of her food is 1 and one quarter is 2. The average is 1.25. Add 1.

items.f: House gecko. Half of her food is moths (level 2) and half is spiders (level 3).
items.b: Level 3.5. The average of 2 and 3 is 2.5. Add 1.

items.f: Rat snake. Half of her food is frogs (level 3) and half is rats who eat grain (level 2).
items.b: Level 3.5. The average of 3 and 2 is 2.5. Add 1.

items.f: Heron. Half of her food is small fish (level 2.5) and half is frogs (level 3).
items.b: Level 3.75. The average of 2.5 and 3 is 2.75. Add 1.

items.f: Hawk. Half of her food is snakes (level 3.5) and half is rats (level 2).
items.b: Level 3.75. The average of 3.5 and 2 is 2.75. Add 1.

items.f: Tuna. Half of her food is sardines (level 2.5) and half is squid (level 3.5).
items.b: Level 4. The average of 2.5 and 3.5 is 3. Add 1.

items.f: A big shark. She eats only tuna, who are level 4.
items.b: Level 5. Her whole diet is level 4, so she is 4 plus 1.

items.f: Meenakshi eats mostly rice, dal and vegetables. Nine tenths of her food is plants and one tenth is curd (level 2).
items.b: Level 2.1. Nine tenths at 1 and one tenth at 2 gives 1.1. Add 1.

items.f: Farhan eats half plants (level 1), a quarter milk (level 2) and a quarter fish (level 3).
items.b: Level 2.75. Half at 1 is 0.5, a quarter at 2 is 0.5, a quarter at 3 is 0.75. The sum is 1.75. Add 1.

rules: A level is 1 plus the average level of what a being eats. Plants and dead plant matter are level 1.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player writes a guess on a slip, such as 2, 2.5 or 3.75. Then everyone shows their slip together.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. The player closest to the answer scores 2 points. Anyone who guessed it exactly scores 3.
If two players are equally close, both score. Any player who can explain the working scores 1 extra point.
With two players, the parent and the child swap roles after every card. The reader never guesses on her own card, so the guesser scores as when playing alone.
Playing alone, write your guess before you look at the back. You score 2 for a guess within 0.25, and 3 for an exact one.
Play ten cards. The player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to beat 20 points.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and make a pile, front side up. Print the score sheet. Read the first rule together.
flow.say: Each card names a living being and what she eats. We guess her level. A level is 1 plus the average level of her food.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. A level is 1 plus the average level of her food.
flow.context: This is the first step of Level Detective. You set up the cards and learn how to work out a level.
flow.parent: No printer? Write the 24 cards by hand on slips of paper. You only need 10 to play. With 3 or 4 players, the reader changes after every card.

flow.do: Play the first five cards. After each one, read the back aloud and check the working. Ask the question below after the third card.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone writes a guess. Show your slips. Now the reader turns the card and reads the working.
flow.kid: Read a card. Write a guess. Show it. Check the back.

ask.q: A level is not always a whole number. Why can a crow be at 2.5?
good: She eats food from two levels.
Half her food is level 1 and half is level 2.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first five cards and learn how to guess.

flow.do: Play the next five cards. Swap the reader's job after each one. Keep score on paper.
flow.say: Keep going. Add up the foods on the card. Take the average. Then add 1.
flow.kid: Play on. Take the average of the foods. Add 1.

check.q: A heron eats half fish at level 2.5 and half frogs at level 3. Which number is closest to her level?
check.why: The average of 2.5 and 3 is 2.75. The heron is one level above her food, so she is at 3.75. If you picked 2.75, you worked out the average of her food but forgot to add 1.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last cards until you have played ten. Add up the points. Then ask the last question.
flow.say: Add up your points. Who found the most? Now look at the cards again. Which animal was highest, and which was lowest?
flow.kid: Add your points. Which card gave the highest level? Which gave the lowest?
flow.parent: A tiger eats deer, who eat plants, so she is at 3. Sea animals often have more levels because the chain starts with tiny algae, and many small steps lie between algae and tuna. Do not worry if your child has not guessed this. It is a thing to wonder about.
flow.think: A tiger is only at level 3. Why do you think a hunter on land is often lower than a hunter in the sea?
flow.context: This is the last step of Level Detective. You count the points and think about what you found.

worksheets.title: From the Sun to the Snake (core)

items.p: What is a producer?
opts: A living being who makes her own food, using light or chemicals
An animal who eats plants
A fungus who feeds on dead leaves
items.why: A producer starts the food chain by making food herself. A plant uses sunlight to make sugar. An animal who eats plants is a consumer, and a fungus who feeds on dead matter is a decomposer.

items.p: In the food chain rice plant, grasshopper, frog, snake, which trophic level is the frog?
opts: Level 3
Level 2
Level 4
items.why: Counting from the producers, the rice plant is level 1, the grasshopper is level 2 and the frog is level 3. The snake is level 4.

items.p: What does the arrow in a food chain show?
opts: The way the energy goes, from the food to the eater
Which animal is stronger
Which animal eats first
items.why: The arrow points from the eaten to the eater, because it shows the way the energy moves. Some children read it as 'eats', which gives the arrow the wrong way round.

items.p: An animal eats a lot of food. Where does most of the energy in that food end up?
opts: As heat, made when her cells use food to run her body
As new body, so she grows a lot
In the air as light
items.why: Most of the energy is used by cells for movement, repair and keeping warm. That use is respiration, and it ends as heat. Only a small part becomes new body.

items.p: A mushroom is a decomposer who eats living plants.
items.why: False. A mushroom is a fungus who digests dead matter outside her body and soaks up the food. Most mushrooms in the home grow on rotting wood or soil.

items.p: Plants respire during the day and at night.
items.why: True. Every living cell respires all the time. In daylight a plant also makes food by photosynthesis, so the two happen together. At night only respiration goes on.

items.p: Cells free the energy in food by a process called ____.
items.why: Respiration uses food and oxygen and gives carbon dioxide, water and heat. It is not the same as breathing, which only brings oxygen in.

items.p: Most of the energy in a food chain finally leaves as ____.
items.why: At every step cells make heat, and heat spreads into the air. That is why the energy cannot be used again by a plant.

items.p: Match each living being to her trophic level in a rice field.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Count the steps from the producer. The rice plant is the producer. Each eater is one step above the food she eats.

items.p: Sort each living being into producer, consumer or decomposer.
items.a: as given
items.why: Producers make their own food. Consumers eat other living beings or their bodies. Decomposers digest dead matter and send the atoms back to the soil, water and air.

items.p: Grass has stored 2000 units of energy in a season. About one tenth passes to the next level each time. How many units reach a frog who eats grasshoppers who ate the grass?
items.why: The grasshoppers get a tenth of 2000, which is 200. The frog gets a tenth of 200, which is 20. This is a rough guess, because real numbers vary.

items.p: Put these in the right order, for the dead-leaf chain in a mangrove.
a: A leaf falls into the mud
Fungi and bacteria soften the leaf
A crab eats the soft leaf
A prawn eats small animals in the mud
items.why: The chain starts with the fallen leaf. It must be softened by microbes before small animals can eat it. Each eater is eaten by the next.

items.p: A vulture eats dead animals. Why is she a consumer and not a decomposer?
items.a: A vulture is an animal who eats the dead body in pieces and digests it inside her own body. A decomposer is a fungus or bacterium who digests dead matter outside her body and soaks it up. Both feed on dead things, but they do it differently.
items.why: A strong answer names the difference: the vulture has a stomach and eats pieces, while decomposers soak up food from outside. It may also say that both help return atoms.

items.p: A friend says: 'When I run, the energy from my rice is used up and gone.' What really happens to it?
items.a: The energy is not used up. It changes form. Some of it moves your muscles, and most of it becomes heat that spreads into the air around you. It cannot be used again by a plant.
items.why: A strong answer says that energy changes form and spreads out as heat, and that it is not destroyed.

items.p: Draw a food chain of four links starting from a rice field. Put an arrow between each link, a level number under each link, and a small red arrow of heat leaving each one.
items.a: Rice plant to grasshopper to frog to snake, with arrows pointing to the eater, levels 1 to 4 beneath, and a red heat arrow from every one.
items.why: A strong drawing points every arrow to the eater, counts the levels from 1, and shows heat leaving from all four links, not only the last.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Mushroom, bread mould, grasshopper, bacteria in compost.
items.a: Grasshopper, because she eats living plants. The other three are decomposers who feed on dead matter.
items.why: Mushrooms, moulds and compost bacteria digest dead matter. A grasshopper is a consumer who eats living leaves.

items.p: Why can the pyramid of numbers for a banyan tree be wide in the middle?
opts: One big tree can feed thousands of small animals
The tree is not a producer
The insects are bigger than the tree
items.why: One banyan has an enormous amount of leaf, so it can feed very many small animals. The count at the bottom is only one, so the numbers pyramid is not a pyramid. Biomass and energy would show a wide base.

items.p: In the open sea, the tiny algae weigh less than the tiny animals who eat them at one moment. Why is the energy pyramid still wide at the bottom?
opts: The algae divide so quickly that they make far more food energy over a year
Algae are heavier than animals
The animals do not need food
items.why: The algae are eaten almost as fast as they grow, so at one moment their weight is small. But they replace themselves every day or two, so over a year they make much more energy than the animals above.

items.p: A hen and a fish weigh the same. Why does the fish turn a larger share of her food into new body?
opts: The hen is warm-blooded and uses most of her food to keep warm
Fish eat more than hens
Hens do not respire
items.why: Warm-blooded animals make heat all the time to stay warm. That uses most of their food. A fish stays close to the water's temperature, so more of her food can become body.

items.p: A crow eats half grain and fruit, which are level 1, and half insects, which are level 2. What is her level?
items.why: The average level of her food is 1.5. She is one step above her food, so her level is 2.5. Choosing 1.5 forgets to add the step for the crow herself.

items.p: An animal keeps the same trophic level all her life.
items.why: False. A level is an average of what she eats. If a crow eats more insects one season, her level goes up a little. If she eats more fruit, it goes down.

items.p: A pyramid of energy can be upside down.
items.why: False. A level can never pass on more energy than it received, and heat leaves at every step. So the energy pyramid is always widest at the bottom.

items.p: A banyan tree's pyramid of ____ is thin at the bottom and wide in the middle.
items.why: The numbers pyramid counts the beings at each level. One tree and thousands of insects makes a spindle shape.

items.p: Match each kind of pyramid to what it measures.
pairs: How many beings are at each level
The weight of living matter at each level
How much energy flows through each level in a year
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each pyramid answers a different question. Only the energy pyramid is always the right way up.

items.p: Sort each of these into where a grasshopper's meal of leaf energy goes.
items: Leaf pieces she did not digest
Leaf edges left uneaten on the plant
items.a: as given
items.why: Movement and keeping cells working use energy that ends as heat. Wastes and uneaten parts still hold energy for decomposers. Only growth and eggs become new body for the next eater.

items.p: A grasshopper takes in 500 units of energy from leaves. 150 units come out as dung and 50 units become new body. How many units did her cells use in respiration?
items.why: She used what is left after the dung and the new body. 500 minus 150 is 350, and 350 minus 50 is 300 units. Most of the food went to run her body and left as heat.

items.p: A peanut holds about 14 kilojoules of energy. The water over a burning peanut caught about 3.5 kilojoules. What fraction of the energy did the water catch?
items.a: one quarter
items.why: 3.5 out of 14 is one quarter, because 3.5 times 4 is 14. The other three quarters warmed the air, the tin and the shield, or left as smoke.

items.p: Put these in order, from the first link to the last, for a food chain in the sea.
items.why: Algae are the producers. Zooplankton graze on them, sardines eat the zooplankton, and tuna eat the sardines.

items.p: Which pyramid is the odd one out, and why? A banyan's numbers pyramid, ticks on a deer in a numbers pyramid, an open-sea biomass pyramid, an open-sea energy pyramid.
items.a: The open-sea energy pyramid, because it is always the right way up. The other three can be upside down.
items.why: Energy cannot grow on its way up a chain. Numbers and biomass depend on how big and how fast-growing the beings are.

items.p: Two friends argue about who runs a forest food web.

views.says: The plants run everything. If there is less rain, there is less grass, fewer deer and fewer tigers, whatever the tigers do.
The hunters run everything. If the tigers go, the deer eat all the young trees, and then the forest changes.
Both matter, and which matters more depends on the place. We need to test each place.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What would you measure to find out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view, gives a reason, and names a test, such as counting plants, deer and hunters in forests with and without tigers.
items.why: Scientists really argue about this. There is no single answer yet, and good thinkers use evidence from each place.

items.p: A tiger is at level 3 but a tuna is at level 4, though both hunt at the top of their food chain. Why do you think they differ?
items.a: The sea chain has more steps. It begins with tiny algae, and many small animals lie between the algae and the tuna. On land the tiger eats deer, who eat plants, so there are fewer steps.
items.why: A strong answer says that the number of steps differs, and may say that sea chains often have more links because the producers are tiny.

items.p: A deer carries 3000 ticks. Draw the pyramid of numbers for the grass, the deer and the ticks, and write what is odd about its shape.
items.a: A thin bar for the grass or a line, a thin bar for one deer, and a very wide bar for the ticks. The shape is upside down at the top, not a pyramid.
items.why: Ticks live on one deer, so their count is far greater than the deer's. Counting beings makes the pyramid odd, and weighing or measuring energy would not.

items.p: Around hot vents at the bottom of the sea, animals live in total darkness. What do the bacteria in their bodies use to make food?
opts: Chemicals from the vent, such as hydrogen sulfide
Sunlight that sinks from the top
Leaves that fall from land
items.why: The bacteria use the energy in chemicals from the vent, a process called chemosynthesis. No sunlight reaches that depth. Their food chain starts with chemical energy from inside the Earth.

items.p: Why do ecologists measure heavy nitrogen in an animal's body?
opts: It becomes a little heavier at each step up the food chain, so it shows her level
It shows how old she is
It shows how fast she can run
items.why: The heavy kind of nitrogen builds up a little at every step. By measuring it, scientists can tell what level an animal has fed at over a long time, even if they never saw her eat.

items.p: In a forest, grazing animals eat only a small share of the leaves while they are alive. What happens to the rest?
opts: It falls and is eaten as dead matter by detritivores and decomposers
It is lost and no one ever uses it
It turns straight into soil without any living being
items.why: Most of the leaves enter the dead-leaf chain. Fungi, bacteria and small animals feed on them. Rotting is something living things do.

items.p: The Earth gives back to space almost as much energy as it gets from the Sun.
items.why: True. The Earth's temperature stays steady because the heat leaving is almost equal to the sunlight arriving. Living things only slow the energy down on its way out.

items.p: Fungi and bacteria are never eaten by anyone.
items.why: False. Tiny worms graze on fungi and bacteria, and springtails eat fungi. Decomposers are food for others too.

items.p: In a food web, ____ go round and round, but energy goes through once.
items.why: A carbon atom can be in the air, in a leaf, in a grasshopper and back in the air again. Energy changes into heat and leaves.

items.p: Match each scientist or team to what they showed.
pairs: Measured the energy at each level in a lake
Showed that bacteria in tube worms make food from chemicals
Argued that hunters keep grazers from eating all the plants
Found that nitrogen gets heavier at each step up a food chain
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four findings are the base of how scientists study the flow of energy through food webs.

items.p: A field receives 10,000 units of sunlight in a season and stores 1 in every 100 in its plants. A grasshopper then gets one tenth of the stored energy. How many units does the grasshopper get?
items.why: One in 100 of 10,000 is 100 units stored in the plants. One tenth of 100 is 10. So the grasshopper gets 10 units out of the 10,000 that fell on the field. Most of the sunlight never became food.

items.p: A hen eats feed holding 400 units of energy in a day. Her egg holds 80 units. What fraction of the feed's energy is in the egg?
items.a: one fifth
items.why: 80 out of 400 is one fifth, because 80 times 5 is 400. The other four fifths went to keep the hen warm and moving, or came out as dung.

items.p: Sort each statement into what scientists agree on or what they still argue about.
items: Heat leaves at every step of a food chain
Plants or hunters run most food webs
Dead leaves feed many food chains
The exact share of mangrove food that comes from mangrove leaves
Atoms are used again and again
How much of the sea's energy passes through viruses
items.a: as given
items.why: Scientists agree on the flow of energy and the recycling of atoms. They are still measuring how much each pathway carries, and which group controls the web.

items.p: Put these in order to follow a bit of rice energy from the Sun to the end.
a: Sunlight falls on a rice leaf
A plant makes sugar and stores energy
The heat spreads into the air and leaves the Earth
items.why: Energy starts as light, is stored as chemical energy, passes to the eater, and finally spreads as heat out to space.

items.p: Which one does not belong, and why? Coal, rice, a peanut, a river pebble.
items.a: The river pebble, because it holds no stored energy from living things. Coal, rice and a peanut all hold energy that plants once caught from sunlight.
items.why: Coal is plant matter that was buried for hundreds of millions of years. Rice and peanuts are plant food. A pebble is a rock.

items.p: A village is arguing about what to farm on its new land.

views.says: Rice, dal and vegetables feed the most people from a field, because each step up the chain wastes energy.
Cows turn straw and grass that people cannot eat into milk, so they add food and waste nothing.
A pond with fish in the flooded paddy gives rice and protein from the same field, without needing a new one.

items.ask: Whose plan would you choose? What would you want to measure first?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a plan, gives a reason, and says what to measure, such as how many people each plan feeds and how much of the food comes from animals.
items.why: People really disagree about this. The best answer for one place may not be best for another.

items.p: A friend says energy is 'passed on' along a food chain, but you say it is not 'kept'. Use the burning peanut to explain what you mean.
items.a: When the peanut burned, its stored energy turned into heat and light. The water caught some of the heat, but most spread into the air. The nut did not keep its energy. In a food chain, each eater receives some energy and lets most of it go as heat.
items.why: A strong answer says that the energy changes form and spreads out, and that at each step much of it becomes heat that is not kept.

items.p: One scientist checks an animal's last meal by looking in her stomach. Another measures the heavy nitrogen in her body. Why might they get different levels?
items.a: The stomach shows only the last meal, which may be unusual. The nitrogen in her body builds up over weeks or months, so it shows what she has eaten over a long time.
items.why: A strong answer says that the stomach shows one meal and the nitrogen shows the long-term diet.

items.p: You want to test whether a compost pile makes heat. Describe a fair test.
items.a: Put a thermometer in the middle of the compost pile and another in a pile of dry sand of the same size next to it. Read both at the same times for three days. If the compost is warmer than the sand and the room, the heat comes from the living things in it.
items.why: A strong answer has a comparison (sand or an empty pile), the same size and place, the same times of reading, and a clear idea of what would show heat made by life.

items.p: Draw the dead-leaf chain of a mangrove creek. Label the detritus, one detritivore, one decomposer and one animal who eats them.
items.a: A fallen mangrove leaf in the mud labelled detritus. A crab labelled detritivore. Fungus or bacteria on the leaf labelled decomposer. A prawn or fish eating small animals from the mud.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the leaf softening first, the crab and microbes feeding on it, and a bigger animal eating them.

experiments.title: A Peanut Full of Sunshine: how much of a bite's energy can you catch?
experiments.question: When a peanut burns under a tin of water, how much does the water warm? And does a foil shield around the flame catch more of the heat?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many degrees will the water warm from one burning peanut? Will the foil shield make it warmer or not? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every trial uses 100 millilitres of water from the same jug, a peanut of about the same size, and a tin held 4 centimetres above the nut. The only thing that changes is the foil shield. Trials 1 and 2 have no shield. Trials 3 and 4 have the shield. We do each twice, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: 8 raw unsalted cashew nuts (they light more easily), or 8 unsalted peanuts (groundnuts) with the skin rubbed off. Use the same kind in every trial. If anyone in your home has a nut allergy, use 8 pea-sized pieces of dry coconut (copra) instead

a small thin metal tin that holds at least 150 millilitres, such as a clean empty condensed-milk tin with the edge smoothed by a grown-up, or a thin steel katori (a thick one soaks up much of the heat)
a digital cooking thermometer with a probe, or a school lab thermometer that reads up to 100 degrees (not a body thermometer)
a measuring cup or a small tumbler marked at 100 millilitres
a jug of cold tap water, so that every trial starts at the same temperature
a steel lid or a small steel plate, a lump of modelling clay and a long steel nail or a metal skewer
kitchen tongs, for holding the tin
kitchen foil, a strip about 12 centimetres wide and 35 centimetres long
a diya or a tea-light candle, and matches (for the grown-up only)
a bowl of water and a wet cloth, kept close, in case a flame spreads
a ruler, a timer, a pencil and the results table
a kitchen scale, if you have one, to weigh 10 nuts together

experiments.safety: A grown-up lights the nut and holds the hot tin. The nut burns with a real flame and spits a little oil. Work on a steel tray, away from curtains, with a bowl of water and a wet cloth close by. Tie back long hair and loose dupattas. Switch off the fan, because moving air blows the flame about. Open a window, because the smoke smells strong. Keep young children a full arm's length back. Never eat a nut that has been burned. Do not leave a burning nut alone. A burned nut stays hot for a minute, so let it cool before touching.
experiments.record: Write the start and end temperatures for each trial and the rise. Work out the average rise for bare and for shielded. Then write one sentence each for: what I think, what I saw, and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you burn a peanut under a tin of water to see how much of its stored energy you can catch as heat. It shows what food energy is, and how much of it escapes.

setup.art: A steel lid with a lump of clay holding a nail, a peanut pressed on the nail point, and a tin with 100 millilitres of water held by kitchen tongs 4 centimetres above the nut.
setup.caption: 1. Press a peanut on a nail in clay. Hold the tin of water 4 centimetres above.

setup.art: A grown-up lighting the peanut with a diya flame while the child holds a thermometer over the tin, with a bowl of water and a wet cloth beside the tray.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up lights the nut. Take the water's start temperature first.

setup.art: The burning peanut under the tin, with a child counting seconds on a timer and a thermometer sticking out of the water.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the tin over the burning nut until the flame goes out. Stir and read the temperature.

setup.art: A foil ring standing around the burning nut with the tin resting on top of the ring and two small notches cut at the bottom of the foil for air.
setup.caption: 4. Repeat with a foil ring around the flame. The tin sits on the ring.

flow.do: Show your child a peanut and a tin of water. Say what you will do. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will burn a peanut under 100 millilitres of water. How many degrees will the water warm? Will a foil shield help? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will burn a peanut under a tin of water. How much will the water warm? Will foil help? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the water will warm by that much?
good: The peanut is hot when it burns.
A flame heats water.
A peanut has a lot of energy inside.

flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, everyone guesses first. Turn the jobs each trial: the grown-up lights, one child times, one reads and stirs, one writes. All children work out the averages. Do not correct the guess. A guess with a reason is a good start. Most children guess 1 or 2 degrees, or 50. The real answer is somewhere between.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Peanut test. You make your guess before the test.

flow.do: Work on a steel tray. A grown-up reads the safety rules first. Press the clay into the lid. Stand the nail in the clay. Press a peanut on to the nail point. Pour 100 millilitres of cold water into the tin. Read the start temperature and write it in the table.
flow.say: A grown-up is in charge of the flame. Press the nail into the clay and a peanut on to the nail. Pour 100 millilitres of water in the tin. Read the temperature and write it down.
flow.kid: A grown-up is in charge of the flame. Set the peanut on the nail. Pour 100 millilitres of water into the tin. Read the temperature.
flow.parent: Bring the tin, the nut and the water to the same room, so the start temperature is the same each time. A peanut with a flat side stands best on the nail. If someone in your home has a nut allergy, use dry coconut for every trial.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the first trial and read the temperature of the water before anything burns.

flow.do: Trial 1 and 2: no shield. A grown-up holds the peanut in the diya flame until it catches. Put it under the tin, held 4 centimetres above with tongs. Time the burn. When the flame goes out, stir the water gently and read the highest temperature. Refill with fresh water for trial 2.
flow.say: Light the nut. It may take up to 30 seconds. Hold the tin 4 centimetres above the flame until it goes out. Then stir the water gently and read the highest number.
flow.kid: A grown-up lights the nut. We hold the tin above it. When the flame dies, we stir and read the temperature.

ask.q: What do you see and smell while the nut burns?
good: A yellow flame.
It crackles and spits oil.
Smoke.
It smells like roasted nuts.

flow.parent: The nut may take a few tries to light, especially in damp weather. Dry the nuts in the sun for an hour first. A cashew lights more easily than a peanut. Let the flame touch an edge. A good peanut burns for 20 to 60 seconds. A rise of about 3 to 10 degrees is typical, but we have not promised it. For a steadier tin, rest it across two upside-down steel katoris about 4 centimetres tall. A black ash left behind is normal. If the rise is under 2 degrees, use only 50 millilitres of water in every trial. Dry the tin before refilling. Do not reuse a half-burned nut.

check.q: The water warmed by 6 degrees. What is the best explanation?
options: Some of the energy stored in the peanut moved into the water as heat.
The peanut made the water hot by touching it.
The tin made the heat.
check.why: A burning peanut changes its stored chemical energy into heat and light. Some heat enters the tin and the water. The nut did not touch the water. If you chose another option, remember that heat can travel through air from a flame to a cold tin.

flow.context: In this step, you do the first two trials with no shield. You find how much a peanut warms the water.

flow.do: Trial 3 and 4: with the shield. Roll the foil strip into a ring about 8 centimetres wide and 4 centimetres tall. Cut two small notches at the bottom for air. Stand the ring round the nail. Light the nut. Rest the tin on top of the ring. Read the water as before.
flow.say: Make a foil ring round the nut, with two notches for air. A grown-up lights the nut. The tin rests on the ring. Read the water when the flame goes out.
flow.kid: Put a foil ring round the nut. A grown-up lights it. Rest the tin on the ring. Read the water.
flow.parent: Keep the notches so the flame can breathe. Without air, the nut goes out. The ring is hot, so let it cool before touching it. Use a fresh nut and fresh water for trial 4.
flow.context: In this step, you repeat the test with a foil shield. You find out if less heat escapes.

flow.do: Work out the average rise for the bare trials and for the shield trials. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Read the nutrition label of the nuts together.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Work out the average rise for each set-up. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the shield trials warmed the water more, because less heat escaped into the room. If the two averages differ by under 1 degree, say the test cannot tell, and repeat it. After they have spoken, explain: the water caught only some of the heat. To find the share, weigh 10 nuts. A nut is typically about 0.6 grams, so weigh yours if you can. The label says about 24 kilojoules in a gram of peanut, so one nut holds about 14 kilojoules. The water caught 100 grams times 4.2 joules times the rise. For a rise of 8 degrees that is 3360 joules, or 3.4 kilojoules, about one quarter. These numbers are rough, because a nut rarely burns fully. The rest warmed the air, the tin and the foil, or left as smoke.
flow.think: Where did the rest of the heat go? How could you catch more of it?

check.q: Water in the shielded set-up warmed more than in the bare set-up. What does that show?
options: The shield stopped some heat from escaping into the room.
The shield made extra energy.
The peanuts in the shield trials were bigger.
check.why: A shield cannot make energy. It only changes where the heat goes. If the water warmed more, less heat escaped into the air. If you chose the third option, check that the nuts were about the same size.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Peanut test. You say what you found and why.

experiments.title: Warm Seeds: do living things give off heat?
experiments.question: Does a box of sprouting moong become warmer than a box of boiled moong or an empty box, if all three sit in the same room?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which box will be warmest after a day? Will any box be warmer than the room? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three boxes have the same size and the same lid. Box A holds soaked, living moong. Box B holds the same amount of moong that has been boiled, so the seeds are dead. Box C is empty. All sit side by side in one big cardboard box, wrapped in a towel. We read the same thermometer in each box at the same times. Box C shows what the room does to a box with nothing alive in it. Box B shows that heat does not come from the moong simply being there.

materials.item: 2 cups of whole green moong with the skin on (about 400 grams). Split moong dal will not sprout
3 steel boxes or plastic tubs of the same size, about 1 litre each, with lids that do not seal tightly and a small hole in each lid for the probe
a digital cooking thermometer with a probe, or a room or aquarium thermometer that reads 0 to 50 degrees
a big cardboard box or a thermocol box that all three tubs fit in, a towel and old newspaper to pack the gaps
a pan and a stove, for a grown-up to boil the moong
a clock or a phone timer, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the moong and drains it. Hot water scalds. Do not eat any moong from this test, because it sits warm for a day. Keep the tubs away from toddlers, because moong seeds are small. Wash your hands after touching the seeds.
experiments.record: Write each temperature in the table. Draw a line graph with one line for each box. Say which box was warmest, and by how many degrees.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you look for heat made by living seeds. Sprouting seeds respire, and respiration gives off heat. You compare living moong, dead moong and an empty box.

schedule.what: In the evening, soak the moong in plenty of water and leave it overnight.
In the morning, drain the moong, boil half, set up the three boxes, and read the first temperatures. Read again at noon and at evening.
Read the temperatures the next morning, about 24 hours after the start. Draw the graph and write what you think.

setup.art: Two cups of whole green moong soaked in a bowl of water overnight, with a label showing day 1.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: soak the moong overnight.

setup.art: Three identical tubs in a row labelled A, B and C. A holds soaked moong, B holds boiled and cooled moong, and C is empty.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: fill tub A with living moong and tub B with boiled, cooled moong. Leave C empty.

setup.art: The three tubs side by side inside a cardboard box wrapped in a towel, with a thermometer lying on top.
setup.caption: 3. Pack the tubs in one box wrapped in a towel.

setup.art: A child pushing a thermometer into the middle of the moong in tub A, with a table beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Read the middle of each tub, always in the same order.

flow.do: On day 1, wash the moong. Put it in a bowl with plenty of water. Leave it overnight. Ask your child to guess the result and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will soak these seeds tonight. Tomorrow we will look for heat. Will living seeds make any heat? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Soak the moong in water tonight. Will living seeds make heat? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Do you think a living seed makes heat? Why?
good: Yes, because all living things make heat.
No, because a seed is asleep.
I am not sure.

flow.parent: A seed is alive and resting. Water wakes it up, and it begins to respire to grow. Test the seeds first. Soak a spoonful in a cup. White tips should show in a day. If not, buy fresh whole moong. With 2 to 4 children, each guesses and draws a graph. They take turns to read the thermometer and write. Do not correct the guess.
flow.wait: Leave the moong in water overnight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Warm Seeds test. You soak the seeds and make a guess.

flow.do: On day 2, drain the moong. Put half in a pan with fresh water and boil it for 10 minutes. A grown-up drains it and cools it fully to room temperature. Fill tub A with the living moong and tub B with the cooled, boiled moong. Leave tub C empty. Put the lids on loosely.
flow.say: A grown-up boils half of the moong for ten minutes. This kills the seeds. When it is cool, put it in tub B. The living moong goes in tub A. Tub C stays empty.
flow.kid: A grown-up boils half the moong. Put the living moong in A and the boiled moong in B. C stays empty.
flow.parent: The boiled moong must be cool before it goes in the tub, or it will start warm. Fill A and B to the same height. A deep tub, about two thirds full, holds heat best. If you have only a little moong, use smaller tubs.
flow.context: In this step, you fill the three tubs. Tub A holds living seeds, tub B dead seeds, and tub C nothing.

flow.do: Put the three tubs in the cardboard box. Wrap the box in a towel. Push the thermometer into the middle of each tub. Wait one minute each and read it. Always go in the order room, A, B, C. Write the numbers in the first row.
flow.say: Put the tubs side by side in the box. Read the room first. Then read A, B and C the same way each time. Write the numbers down.
flow.kid: Put the tubs in the box. Read the room, then A, B and C. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Pack the gaps with crumpled newspaper. Wipe the thermometer between tubs. The first readings should be almost the same. If A and B differ by more than 1 degree, wait 20 minutes and read again.

check.q: Why does the test include a box with boiled moong?
options: To show that heat does not come from moong that is only sitting there.
To make the test longer.
To get extra moong.
check.why: Boiled moong is full of the same food as living moong, but it is dead. If it stayed as cool as the empty tub, then the heat must come from life. If you chose another option, remember that a fair test changes one thing at a time.

flow.context: In this step, you pack the tubs and take the first readings. These are your starting temperatures.

flow.do: Read the room and the three tubs again at noon and at evening. Always use the same order and wait the same time. Write the numbers. Do not open the tubs for longer than you need.
flow.say: Read the room, A, B and C again. Write the numbers. Keep the lids closed between readings.
flow.kid: Read all four numbers again. Write them down. Close the lids.
flow.parent: Keep the box in the coolest, shadiest room, away from the fan and the sun. In hot weather, tub B may warm too, and smell sour, as microbes grow. A rise of 1 or 2 degrees is typical, and it may be zero. A rise is real if the thermometer gave the same number in all three tubs at the start. Moong that is sprouting well will have small white tips by the evening. If A is no warmer than C, add more moong, use a smaller tub, or wrap the box with another towel.
flow.context: In this step, you take more readings during the day. A warm rise builds slowly.

flow.do: On day 3, read all four numbers again. Draw a line graph, one line for each tub. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then throw the moong away.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each tub. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that tub A warmed more than B and C because the living seeds respire. After they have spoken, explain: respiration frees the energy in food, and some of it always turns into heat. Tub B may warm slightly after a day if microbes start to grow on the boiled moong. That is also respiration. If A is no warmer than C, say so. A small tub of seeds may not make enough heat to measure, and a larger heap would. A compost heap shows it clearly.
flow.think: A compost heap can get hot enough to steam. What do you think is happening inside it?

check.q: Tub A is 2 degrees warmer than tub C. What does this show?
options: Living seeds gave off heat as they respired.
Moong makes energy out of nothing.
The towel made tub A warmer.
check.why: Cells use food to free energy, and some of it becomes heat. The energy was in the seed's stored food. The towel wrapped all three tubs, so it cannot explain why only A was warmer.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Warm Seeds test. You say what you found and why.

activities.title: Pyramid Strips: numbers, weight and energy

materials.item: A4 paper, ruler, scissors, glue and a pencil
coloured pencils
the data cards in the steps (made-up round numbers that show a real pattern)

activities.record: Glue your pyramids on one sheet. Under each, write one sentence about its shape.
activities.context: In this activity, you build three kinds of pyramid from paper strips. They show why a pyramid of numbers can be upside down but a pyramid of energy cannot.

setup.art: Four paper strips of different widths glued one above the other and centred, forming a pyramid, with the numbers 1000, 100, 10 and 1 written on them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut strips whose width shows the number. Centre them one above another.

setup.art: A spindle-shaped drawing made from strips for a banyan tree, with a very thin line at the bottom for one tree and a wide strip above it for insects.
setup.caption: 2. Make a pyramid of numbers for a banyan tree. It does not look like a pyramid.

setup.art: A pyramid of energy made from four strips, widest at the bottom, with the label energy in a year.
setup.caption: 3. Make an energy pyramid for the sea. Compare it with the weight pyramid.

flow.do: Read the numbers for a grass field out loud. Grass plants 1000. Grasshoppers 100. Frogs 10. Snakes 1. Cut four strips 1 centimetre wide for every 100 beings. So grass is 10 centimetres wide. Grasshoppers are 1 centimetre. Frogs and the snake are so thin that you can draw them as lines. Glue the strips in a pyramid, centred.
flow.say: These are made-up numbers for a grass field. We will draw how wide each level is. The widest strip is the grass. The snake is just a line.
flow.kid: Cut a wide strip for the grass. Make the grasshoppers narrower. Make the frogs and snake thin lines. Glue them in a pyramid.

good: A pyramid.
Wide at the bottom and narrow at the top.

flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each makes one pyramid, and you glue them on one big sheet. One child checks the widths with the ruler. The made-up numbers keep the sums easy. If cutting a 1 millimetre strip is hard, draw the thin levels with a pen.
flow.context: In this step, you make a pyramid of numbers for a grass field. It is the usual pyramid shape.

flow.do: First sketch the shape you expect. Now do a banyan tree. One tree. 1000 insects that eat her leaves. 20 birds that eat the insects. 1 hawk. Use the same rule, 1 centimetre for every 100. The tree is a line. The insects are 10 centimetres wide. Glue them in a pile and look at the shape.
flow.say: First sketch the shape you expect. Now a banyan tree. There is one tree, but 1000 insects live on her leaves. Make the strips. What shape do you get?
flow.kid: Make strips for one banyan tree. One tree is a line. Then 1000 insects, 20 birds and 1 hawk. What shape is it?
flow.parent: The shape is thin, wide, thin, thinner. This is correct. Counting the number of beings makes the tree look unimportant, even though she feeds everyone.

check.q: The banyan pyramid of numbers is wide in the middle. What does that tell us?
options: One big producer can feed very many small animals.
The insects are more important than the tree.
The banyan tree is not a producer.
check.why: A big tree has a large amount of leaf to share. So the number of animals is high even though there is only one tree. A pyramid of numbers can hide how important the tree is.

flow.context: In this step, you make a pyramid of numbers for a banyan tree. It is not a pyramid.

flow.do: Now the open sea. These made-up weights are in tonnes, at one moment. Tiny algae 2, tiny animals 5, small fish 3, tuna 1. Use 1 centimetre for each tonne and glue the strips. Then make a second pyramid for the energy in a year: 1000, 100, 10 and 1. Use 1 centimetre for every 100 units. Compare the two.
flow.say: In the open sea, the algae are eaten as fast as they grow. At one moment they weigh less than the tiny animals who eat them. Make that pyramid. Then make the energy pyramid.
flow.kid: Make a weight pyramid for the sea. The algae are narrow. Then make the energy pyramid. Compare them.

ask.q: Why is the energy pyramid still the right way up?
good: The algae make a lot of food over a year.
Energy cannot grow on the way up.
Each level passes on less.

flow.parent: The weight pyramid is narrow at the very bottom, because the algae are eaten as quickly as they grow. The energy pyramid is wide at the bottom, because the algae make far more food each year than any other level. The numbers are made up to show the pattern.
flow.context: In this step, you make a pyramid of weights for the open sea. You also make a pyramid of energy. Only one of them can be upside down.

activities.title: Who lives in the dead leaves? A funnel trap for tiny animals

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle of 1.5 or 2 litres, with the top third cut off by a grown-up
a square of mosquito net or window net, or a tea strainer, to sit inside the funnel
2 cups of leaf litter, compost or moist soil from the bottom of a potted plant
a jar or a cup with a little damp tissue paper in the bottom
a desk lamp with a bright bulb (an old filament bulb or a CFL is best; an LED stays cool, so it works slowly), or strong sun on a window sill
a magnifying glass, and a white plate or sheet of paper

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottle. The bulb gets hot, so keep it 15 centimetres above the soil (10 for an LED) and away from the plastic. Do not touch it. Stay in the room while it is on. Centipedes can bite, so lift nothing with your fingers. Use a spoon or paper strip. Wash your hands after touching soil or compost. Do not touch any animals with your bare hands.
activities.record: Draw the animals you find, and write how many you counted and what each might eat.
activities.context: In this activity, you find the small animals that live on dead leaves. They are the first eaters in the dead-leaf chain, and a lamp drives them out of the soil into a cup.

setup.art: A bottle top turned upside down as a funnel, with a net inside and a jar of damp tissue underneath.
setup.caption: 1. Turn the cut bottle top upside down as a funnel. Put the net inside.

setup.art: Leaf litter in the funnel and a desk lamp above it, shining down.
setup.caption: 2. Put the leaf litter in. Shine the lamp from above.

setup.art: A child looking at tiny animals in the jar through a magnifying glass, on a white plate.
setup.caption: 3. After 1 hour, look at what fell into the jar.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the top third off the bottle. Turn the top upside down and stand it in a jar. Put the net inside. Add the leaf litter. Ask your child to guess what will fall into the jar and why.
flow.say: We will see who lives in the dead leaves. Light and warmth dry the leaves from the top. What do you think will fall into the jar? Why?
flow.kid: Make a funnel with the bottle top. Put the leaves in. What will fall into the jar? Why?
flow.parent: The best litter is damp, brown and crumbly, from under a tree, from a compost pot or from a kitchen compost bin. Fresh potting mix often has almost nothing alive. If your soil is dry, mist it. With 2 to 4 children, make one funnel each with a different litter, such as under a tree, a compost pot and dry soil. The animals are tiny, so use the magnifying glass.
flow.context: This is the first step of the funnel trap. You set it up and make a guess.

flow.do: Put the lamp 15 centimetres above the leaves and switch it on. Set a timer for 1 hour. Do not move the funnel. Let your child draw what they think they will see.
flow.say: Turn the lamp on. The animals dislike the dry heat, so they crawl down and fall into the jar. We wait one hour.
flow.kid: Switch the lamp on. Wait 1 hour. Do not touch the funnel.
flow.parent: Keep the lamp away from anything that burns. A paper towel under the jar is fine. If you see nothing, wait another hour. A big catch needs 2 hours.
flow.context: In this step, you start the trap. The lamp pushes the animals down into the jar.

flow.do: Put a little of what fell into the jar on the white plate. Look with the magnifying glass. Count how many kinds you see. Draw two. Say what each one might be eating.
flow.say: Look at the plate. Count the kinds of animals. Draw two of them. What might each one eat?
flow.kid: Tip the jar on to the plate. Look with the lens. Count the kinds. Draw two.

ask.q: Which of these animals eats leaves, and which eats other animals?
good: The ones with small mouths eat leaves or fungus.
The fast ones with big jaws eat other animals.

flow.parent: You may find springtails, which are tiny and jump, mites, small pale worms, tiny beetles, centipedes and ants. Many are detritivores. A fast-moving one with big jaws, like a centipede, is probably a hunter. If almost nothing fell, that is a result too. Count each funnel on its own and compare. Try compost or leaf litter from outside.

check.q: Why do the animals fall down into the jar?
options: The lamp dries the top of the leaves, so they move away from the heat and dryness.
The lamp pulls them down.
They want to fall into the jar.
check.why: Soil animals like damp places. When the lamp dries and warms the top, they crawl down, through the net, and into the jar. The lamp does not pull them. They move away from the dry heat.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the animals that fell into the jar. These animals eat dead leaves or each other.
flow.think: Which litter gave the most animals? Why do you think so?

activities.title: The Level of My Lunch

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a plate of your own lunch, or a photograph of one

activities.record: Draw your lunch with an arrow from each food to the being it came from. Write the level number next to each food.
activities.context: In this activity, you find the trophic level of each food on your lunch plate, and then of yourself. Most animals eat at more than one level, and so do you.

setup.art: A thali with rice, sambar, a vegetable, curd and a fish fry, with a label on each food showing the being it came from.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your lunch. Write what each food came from.

setup.art: A list with the level numbers beside each food: rice 1, sambar 1, curd 2, fish fry 2.5.
setup.caption: 2. Write a level number next to each food.

setup.art: A short sum showing the four numbers added and divided, and the answer plus one.
setup.caption: 3. Add the numbers, divide, and add 1 to find your own level.

flow.do: Look at a lunch plate, yours or one from a photograph. List each food. For each, write what living being it came from. Rice came from a rice plant. Curd came from a cow. A fish fry came from a fish.
flow.say: Look at the food on your plate. Write each food on a list. Next to it, write the living being it came from.
flow.kid: List the foods on your plate. Next to each, write the living being it came from.
flow.parent: A plain vegetarian plate is fine. Its level will be low, and the method is the point. Use real foods from your own lunch. A thali with rice, sambar, a vegetable, curd and an egg or fish is a good example.
flow.context: In this step, you list your lunch and find where each food came from.

flow.do: Write a level for each food. Plants are level 1. A cow eats grass, so she is level 2, and so are milk and curd. A hen eats half grain and half insects, and she is about 2.25. A sardine is about 2.5. Egg: 2.25. Fish fry: 2.5.
flow.say: A food has the level of the being it came from. Plants are level 1. Cows are level 2. Hens are 2.25 and sardines are 2.5.
flow.kid: Write a level beside each food. Plants are 1. Cow's milk and curd are 2. Eggs are 2.25. Sardines are 2.5.
flow.parent: These levels come from the Level Detective game. If you do not have a level for an animal, ask a grown-up to guess, using what she eats.

check.q: A person eats rice, dal and curd in equal amounts. Rice and dal are level 1 and curd is level 2. What is the average level of the food?
options: About 1.3
About 2
About 3
check.why: Rice 1 plus dal 1 plus curd 2 is 4. Four divided by 3 is about 1.3. The average level of the food is 1.3, and the person herself is one level above it, about 2.3.

flow.context: In this step, you give each food a level number. The number is the level of the being it came from.

flow.do: First guess your own level. Then add the level numbers of all the foods. Divide by the number of foods. This is the average level of your food. Add 1. That is your level for this lunch. Compare it with your family's.
flow.say: Add up the numbers. Divide by how many foods there are. Add 1. That is your level for this lunch.
flow.kid: Add the numbers. Divide by how many foods. Add 1. That is your level.
flow.parent: For a lunch of rice 1, sambar 1, curd 2 and fish fry 2.5, the sum is 6.5. Dividing by 4 gives 1.6, and adding 1 gives 2.6. This treats every food as an equal share. A real plate has more rice than curd, so your true level is a little lower. With 2 to 4 children, each works out one plate and you compare. Most people land between 2 and 3. Scientists estimate that people around the world average about 2.2.
flow.think: If you swapped the fish fry for a vegetable, what would your level be?
flow.context: In this step, you work out your own trophic level for one lunch.

projects.record: Write the pie chart numbers and your family's average level. Write one sentence about what surprised you.

flow.do: On day 1, list every food your family eats. Write each food and a rough amount, such as 3 spoons or 2 pieces. Add drinks like milk and buttermilk. Ask your child to guess how many foods come from plants.
flow.say: Today we write down everything we eat. Next to each food, write how much. How many foods will come from plants? Why?

flow.do: On day 2, next to each food, write the being it came from. Write its level, using the Level Detective cards. Skip salt. Count how many foods are at level 1, at level 2 and above. Add the levels and divide by the number of foods. Add 1.

flow.parent: Rice, wheat, dal, vegetables, fruit and oil are level 1. Milk, curd and ghee are level 2. Eggs are 2.25. A chicken meal is 2.25 as the food. Small sea fish are about 2.5. A bigger fish such as a tuna is 4. Salt does not count. A count of foods treats a pinch of ghee like a bowl of rice. For a fairer answer, count each food once for every spoon or piece. Then work out the average again.

flow.do: On day 3, draw a pie chart of the foods by level. Use three colours: level 1, level 2, and above 2. Then draw one chain from the Sun to a favourite meal. Put a small red arrow of heat leaving each step.

flow.kid: Draw a pie chart. Then draw a chain from the Sun to your favourite meal. Add red heat arrows.
flow.think: What is the level of your whole family's food? What would change it most?

challenges.title: Feed the Village: twelve fields, eighty mouths
challenges.problem: A village of 80 people has 12 fields. Each field can grow rice, grass for cows, or fish in a pond. Plan the fields to feed everyone for one month. At least one tenth of the food must come from milk, fish or eggs, because people need more than rice. Use these made-up numbers. One rice field feeds 8 people for a month. One grass field for cows feeds 1 person for a month with milk. One fish pond feeds 3 people for a month. If you keep at least one grass field, the straw from each 2 rice fields feeds the cows and adds 1 more person-month of milk, up to 4 more.
constraints: You have exactly 12 fields, and each field does one job.
You must feed at least 80 people-months.
At least 8 of those people-months must come from milk, fish or eggs.
Show your sums on paper, one line for each kind of field.
These numbers are made up, but they keep the true pattern: animals give back less than plants.
materials: 12 paper squares or bottle caps to be fields
three colours of pencil: one for rice, one for grass, one for fish
paper and a pencil to write sums
general: Grow rice in 9 fields and keep 3 fish ponds. Rice feeds 72 and the ponds feed 9. That is 81 people-months, and 9 come from fish. It works, and it needs no cows.

Grow rice in 10 fields, 1 fish pond and 1 grass field. Rice feeds 80, the pond 3 and the grass 1. Straw adds 4, which is the most it can add. That is 88, and 8 come from animals. It works with a little to spare.
Grow rice in 9 fields, 1 fish pond and 2 grass fields. Rice feeds 72, the pond 3 and the grass 2. Straw adds 4. That is 81, and 9 come from animals. It works.
Grow rice in all 12 fields. That feeds 96, but nothing comes from milk, fish or eggs. It fails the rule for animal foods.
creative: Keep ducks in the rice fields. Ducks eat insects and snails and leave dung that feeds the rice. This is done in Kuttanad in Kerala.
Raise fish in the flooded rice fields, as in pokkali fields near Kochi. One field then gives both rice and fish.
Feed hens on kitchen scraps, not grain, so no field is needed for them.
Plant a row of banana or coconut trees along the field edges, to give food without using a whole field.
challenges.your_turn: Try your own plan with the same 12 fields. Add one change from the creative list. Say how many people-months it feeds, how many come from animals, and what you would do if a flood washed away two rice fields.
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge about food energy. It uses made-up numbers to show why animals give back less than plants, and why cows and fish can still be a good choice.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Lay out the 12 squares. Ask your child to guess what mix of fields will feed 80 people, and why.
flow.say: We have 12 fields and 80 people. Rice feeds 8 for each field. What mix of fields do you think will work? Why?
flow.kid: We have 12 fields and 80 people. Rice feeds 8 for each field. What mix will work?

good: Rice alone would not meet the rule for milk, fish or eggs.
People need more than rice.

flow.context: This is the first step of Feed the Village. You read the problem and make a guess.

flow.do: Try three plans. For each, write the number of rice, grass and fish fields. Work out the people-months from rice, fish, grass and straw. Check that the total is at least 80, and at least 8 come from animals.
flow.say: Try three plans. Add up the people-months. Does each plan feed 80? Do 8 come from milk or fish?
flow.kid: Try three plans. Add up the people-months. Check each rule.
flow.parent: The best plans keep 9 or 10 rice fields, with 1 or 2 grass fields and one pond if there are enough fields. The straw makes the cows worth keeping, because they turn something people cannot eat into milk. Help your child with the straw rule, which is the hard part.
flow.context: In this step, you test three plans against the rules and your sums.

flow.do: Pick your best plan. Write it as a sum. Then try the 'your turn' challenge with a change from the creative list. Say which plan wastes the least energy, and why.
flow.say: Choose your best plan. Write it as a sum. Then add one creative change. Which plan wastes the least energy?
flow.kid: Pick your best plan. Add one creative change. Which wastes the least?

flow.context: This is the last step of Feed the Village. You choose a plan and say why it works.

quiz.p: Which sentence best describes a food chain?
opts: It shows the path of energy from a producer to the animals that eat her
It lists every animal in a forest
It shows which animals are friends
quiz.why: A food chain follows the energy from the producer to each eater. A list of animals is not a chain, and the arrows show eating, not friendship.

quiz.p: An animal eats 100 units of energy. Which statement is most likely true?
opts: Only a small part becomes new body that the next eater can use
Nearly all of it becomes new body
None of it becomes heat
quiz.why: Most of the food is used by cells and ends as heat. A small part grows the body, and some leaves as dung. So the next eater gets only a small part.

quiz.p: Why do hunters at the top of a food chain need a large area to live in?
opts: Little energy reaches the top, so many levels of plants and animals are needed beneath them
They like to walk far
Plants grow slowly near hunters
quiz.why: Each step loses most of the energy. A hunter needs the food of many levels below her, so she needs a large area with a lot of plants.

quiz.p: A pyramid of numbers for one oak tree and the insects living on her is wide in the middle. What does this show?
opts: Counting beings can hide how much a big producer gives
The oak is not a producer
Insects weigh more than the oak
quiz.why: A single tree can feed thousands of insects. Counting gives one at the bottom, so the shape looks odd. A pyramid of energy would be wide at the bottom.

quiz.p: A warm-blooded hunter and a cold-blooded hunter eat the same weight of food. Who makes more new body?
opts: The cold-blooded hunter, because the warm-blooded one spends more food on keeping warm
The warm-blooded hunter, because she is bigger
They make the same amount
quiz.why: Keeping the body warm uses a lot of food and ends as heat. Cold-blooded animals do less of this, so more of their food can become body.

opts: Dead leaves, wood, dung and dead bodies, broken into pieces
Only the soil under a tree
A kind of living fungus
quiz.why: Detritus is the dead matter that detritivores and decomposers eat. Soil is not only detritus, and a fungus is a living decomposer.

quiz.p: In a mangrove creek, why would cutting the trees reduce the number of prawns?
opts: Fewer leaves fall, so there is less food at the start of the dead-leaf chain
Prawns eat the trees directly
The water becomes colder
quiz.why: Fallen leaves feed crabs and small animals, which feed prawns. Cutting the trees cuts the supply of leaves, so each level below the prawns has less food.

quiz.p: What happens to the atoms in a dead leaf?
opts: Decomposers and other eaters pass them on, and they return to the soil, water and air
They disappear
They are turned into energy and leave as light
quiz.why: Atoms are not destroyed. They move from leaf to fungus to animal and back to the air and soil. They are used again and again.

quiz.p: Which statement about energy and atoms is correct?
opts: Atoms go round and round, but energy flows through and leaves as heat
Energy goes round and atoms leave
Both stay inside living things for ever
quiz.why: Atoms are used again and again. Energy arrives as light and leaves as heat, so life needs a fresh supply of sunlight every day.

quiz.p: Why must a fair test of burning peanuts use the same amount of water and the same height for the tin?
opts: So that only one thing changes and any difference comes from that one thing
So that the nuts burn faster
So that the flame is bigger
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing at a time. If the water or the height changes too, we cannot tell which change caused the different result.

quiz.p: The water over a burning nut caught only a quarter of the nut's energy. Which statement is the best explanation?
opts: The rest of the heat warmed the air, the tin and the smoke
A nut holds less energy than the label says
Three quarters of the energy was destroyed
quiz.why: Energy is not destroyed. The rest of the heat spread into the air and the tin, so the water could not catch it all. This is a small version of the loss at every step of a food chain.

quiz.p: Scientists disagree about whether plants from below or hunters from above run a food web. What is the best way to settle it?
opts: Measure plants, grazers and hunters in many places and compare them
Ask the oldest scientist
Choose the view that most people like
quiz.why: A real argument in science is settled by evidence from many places. The answer may differ from one place to another.

applications: Farmers choose crops and animals by asking how much food energy each field can really give. Rice and ragi give more energy per hectare than cattle fed on grain.
Fish farmers in Kerala and Andhra Pradesh feed fish and prawns as low on the chain as they can, because every step up wastes energy.
Biogas plants and composting turn the energy in dung and kitchen waste into gas and heat that families use, using the decomposer chain on purpose.
Conservation planners count the energy at the bottom of the web to decide how many tigers a forest can support.
Fishing rules, such as a break during the monsoon, protect the lower levels so that bigger fish can feed.
Dairy farmers feed cows straw and grass that people cannot eat, and get milk, which is a way of turning energy people cannot use into food people can.
Insulated lunch boxes and thermoses work by slowing the heat's escape, the same escape that every body in a food chain has.
Scientists measure what fish and sea birds eat by the heavy nitrogen in their bodies, to learn whether a fishery is still healthy.
Wetland and mangrove protection, such as at Pichavaram and in the Sundarbans, keeps the dead-leaf chain that feeds fish.
Cooks and nutritionists measure food in kilojoules or kilocalories, the same energy units that scientists use to measure a food chain.

open_questions.q: How much of the food in a mangrove creek really comes from the mangrove leaves, and how much comes from algae and plankton?
open_questions.why_open: Studies in different places give different answers, and the answer seems to change with the tide, the season and the creek.

open_questions.q: Do plants or hunters run most food webs?
open_questions.why_open: Some places seem to be run from below and some from above. Scientists do not yet know why, or how it will change as the climate changes.

open_questions.q: How much of the energy of the sea passes through viruses and microbes that we cannot see?
open_questions.why_open: These tiny beings are hard to count and to watch. Scientists have estimates, but new studies keep changing the picture.

open_questions.q: How many of the links in a food web are parasites, and what do they change?
open_questions.why_open: Parasites are hard to find and hard to count. Only a few food webs have been studied with parasites included.

open_questions.q: Could there be food chains that run on chemical energy on other worlds, such as under the ice of Europa, a moon of Jupiter?
open_questions.why_open: We have found hot vents on Earth where life lives without sunlight. Nobody has yet looked beneath the ice of other worlds.

open_questions.q: As the climate warms, will animals turn a smaller or a larger share of their food into body?
open_questions.why_open: Cold-blooded animals depend on their surroundings for warmth, so warming changes how fast they use their food. Scientists are still measuring this in many animals.

maths.problem: In your peanut test, 100 grams of water warmed by 8 degrees. It takes about 4 joules to warm 1 gram of water by 1 degree. How many joules did the water catch?
maths.explain: Multiply the three numbers. 100 times 8 is 800. 800 times 4 is 3200. So the water caught about 3200 joules, or 3.2 kilojoules.
maths.context: In the Peanut test, you read a thermometer. Here you turn that reading into an amount of energy.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying turns a thermometer reading into an amount of energy, so that you can compare it with the energy in the nut.

maths.problem: The peanut held about 14,000 joules and the water caught 3500. A friend says most of the heat was lost. Is she right? What fraction was lost?
maths.explain: 3500 out of 14,000 is one quarter, because 3500 times 4 is 14,000. So the water caught one quarter and three quarters went elsewhere. She is right.
maths.context: In the Peanut test, the water caught only some of the nut's heat. This question asks how much.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells you how big a part is compared to the whole, so you can see how much of the energy escaped.

maths.problem: In a grass field the grass holds 2000 units of energy, the grasshoppers 200 and the frogs 20. If the pattern continues, how many units does a snake who eats the frogs get? Why does the pattern stop being useful for very high levels?
maths.answer: 2 units. The numbers get so small that there is not enough food for a large animal.
maths.explain: Each level has a tenth of the one below. A tenth of 20 is 2. Two units are too little to support a big hunter, so food chains stop after a few levels.
maths.context: In Pyramid Strips, each level had a tenth of the one below. This question continues that pattern.
maths.why_maths: A pattern lets you guess what comes next, and see when the guess shows a limit.

maths.problem: In the Peanut test, the bare set-up gave rises of 5 and 7 degrees. The shielded set-up gave rises of 9 and 11 degrees. The two trials of each set-up differ by 2 degrees. The averages differ by 4. Does the shield really make a difference?
maths.answer: Yes, probably. The gap between the set-ups is bigger than the gap between two trials of the same set-up.
maths.explain: The averages are 6 and 10, so they differ by 4 degrees. Two trials of the same set-up differ by only 2. A difference bigger than the usual wobble between trials is more likely to be real.
maths.context: In the Peanut test, you do each set-up twice. Here you decide if the difference between set-ups is real.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a difference with the wobble between repeats shows whether a result is likely to be real.

maths.problem: A hen eats 3 parts grain, which is level 1, for every 1 part of insects, which is level 2. What is her level? Show how you work it out.
maths.explain: Out of 4 parts, 3 are level 1 and 1 is level 2. The total is 3 plus 2, which is 5. Five divided by 4 is 1.25. Add 1 for the hen herself, and she is at 2.25.
maths.context: In Level Detective, you work out a level from what a being eats. This question uses a ratio.
maths.why_maths: A ratio tells you how much of each food is eaten, so you can work out an average level.

maths.problem: In Feed the Village, you plant 9 rice fields, 1 fish pond and 2 grass fields. How many people-months does the plan feed, and does it follow the rule that at least 8 come from animal foods?
maths.answer: 81 people-months, and 9 come from animals. Yes, it follows the rule.
maths.explain: Rice feeds 9 times 8, which is 72. The pond feeds 3 and the grass feeds 2. The straw from 9 rice fields adds 4, the most it can add. The total is 72 plus 3 plus 2 plus 4, which is 81. Animal foods are 3 plus 2 plus 4, which is 9.
maths.context: In Feed the Village, you plan twelve fields. This question checks one plan against the rules.
maths.why_maths: Checking a plan against rules, one rule at a time, is how you solve a problem with limits.

maths.problem: In the Warm Seeds test, tub A read 28, 29, 30 and 31 degrees at four times. The room read 27, 27, 28 and 27. How much warmer than the room was tub A each time? What does the pattern say about the heat?
maths.answer: 1, 2, 2 and 4 degrees warmer. The gap is growing, so the seeds keep making heat.
maths.explain: Subtract the room from tub A each time. 28 minus 27 is 1, 29 minus 27 is 2, 30 minus 28 is 2, and 31 minus 27 is 4. The gap grows, which suggests living seeds keep making heat that builds up.
maths.context: In the Warm Seeds test, you read tub A and the room at four times. This question compares them.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the room's temperature shows how much extra warmth the seeds made, and a growing gap shows a pattern.

maths.problem: In the energy pyramid for a field, the grass holds 1000 units, and the frogs hold 10. What percent of the grass's energy reaches the frogs? Would a fish farm that feeds fish on algae directly pass on more or less?
maths.answer: 1 percent. A fish farm that feeds fish on algae directly skips a level, so the farm passes on more of the original energy.
maths.explain: 10 out of 1000 is 1 out of 100, which is 1 percent. If the fish eat algae directly, they are only one step from the producers. One fewer step means one fewer loss, so more of the algae's energy reaches them.
maths.context: In Pyramid Strips, you saw energy shrink up a pyramid. Here you give the shrinking as a percent.
maths.why_maths: A percent lets you compare how much of the energy reaches different levels on the same scale.
