roots.context: We have followed the Sun's energy along food chains and watched it turn into heat. Now we ask what this tells us about what a living body is, and who we are.

deep_truth.truth: Energy is not kept in a food chain. It passes through, and at every step most of it turns into heat. A living body is not a store of energy. It is a pattern that lasts only while energy keeps flowing through it, like a flame.
deep_truth.habit: We talk as if a body 'has' energy and 'uses it up', like petrol in a tank, and as if the animal at the top has collected the most. But energy is never used up. It only changes form and spreads out as heat. What a body keeps is a way of letting energy pass.
deep_truth.evidence: The burning peanut gave its stored energy to the water, the air and the tin, and none of it stayed in the nut. Lindeman found less energy at every level of a lake, and heat leaves the Earth as fast as sunlight arrives. Living cells give off heat every second they are alive, and a body that stops taking in energy stops being alive.

three.who_am_i: You are not a box that holds energy. You are a pattern that lasts while sunlight, through plants and food, keeps flowing through you.
three.what_is_life: Life is energy passing through matter in a particular shape. Every being, from a bacterium to a tiger, keeps that shape going for a while by taking energy in and letting heat out.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth is a place where the Sun's light is slowed down on its way back to space. Every green leaf, every grasshopper and every mangrove crab is part of that slowing down.

roots.thread: Sunlight arrives all as one stream. A leaf catches a small part, a caterpillar takes a small part of that, and a bird a small part of that again. At each step the stream turns into many bodies, each in a different shape, and at each step heat leaves and joins the sky. The Earth then gives back to space almost as much as it received. Nothing in the chain keeps the energy, and nothing in the chain could live without it. The many bodies are one flow, seen at different places along its way.

teachings.teaching: A son, Bhrigu, asks his father Varuna to teach him what the ultimate is. The father says to look at food. Bhrigu finds that all beings are born from food, live by food, and go back into food.
teachings.link: This is the food chain and the dead-leaf chain in one line. A body comes from food, and when it dies it becomes food again for others.

teachings.teaching: The verse says that all this world is pervaded by one reality. It then says to enjoy what is given by letting go, and not to covet anyone's wealth.
teachings.link: In a food chain, no one holds the energy for long. Each eater receives, uses and lets go. The heat she lets go is what the next living thing, the sky, receives.

teachings.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.21, a Jain text by Umaswati
teachings.teaching: The sutra says 'parasparopagraho jivanam', which is often translated as 'living beings support one another'.
teachings.link: A mangrove leaf feeds a crab, who feeds a prawn, who feeds a heron. Each being lives because others give their bodies, wastes and warmth.

science.text: Energy is never made or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. Sunlight becomes chemical energy in a leaf, and chemical energy becomes heat in every cell.

Some physicists, following Erwin Schrödinger in 1944 and Ilya Prigogine later, say a living thing is a pattern that keeps itself going only by taking in energy and giving out heat. How exactly life began as such a pattern is still open.

other_view.view: Energy flow is a useful way to count, but it is our way of drawing nature. A forest has no goal of passing on energy. They say it is better to study how species affect each other, because a tiny predator can change a whole web without moving much energy.

practice.title: One slow mouthful
practice.say: Take a small piece of fruit or a spoon of rice. Before you eat, hold your other hand against your cheek and feel your own warmth. Now put the food in your mouth and chew it slowly for twenty seconds. Think about where the food was a few weeks ago. It was in a field, in the sunlight. Think about your warm hand. Some of that sunlight is now warming it. Then breathe out slowly and feel the warm air leave you.
practice.kid: Feel your cheek with your hand. It is warm. Now chew one bite slowly. This food held sunlight. Now some of it is warming you. Breathe out and feel the warm air go.

ask: If none of the energy stays in you, what is it that stays?
When you die, the atoms and the energy go on to others. What stops?
Is the heat that leaves a body lost, or given?
roots.art: A child holding a bite of rice beside a warm cheek, with a thin line of golden light running from a faraway Sun, through a rice plant, to the child, and wavy heat lines going up from the child into the sky.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet burned or sprouted at home. The Peanut test needs a grown-up for the flame, a thin metal tin and a digital cooking thermometer. A rise of 3 to 10 degrees is the usual result with 100 millilitres, and the steps say what to do if it is smaller, if the nut will not light, and if anyone is allergic to nuts. The energy of one peanut (about 14 kilojoules from 0.6 grams and a label of 24 kilojoules per gram) is an estimate, so the quarter caught by the water is a rough figure. Warm Seeds may give only a 1 to 2 degree rise or none in small tubs, and the steps say how to repeat it. The funnel trap needs damp leaf litter or compost, and a sterile potting mix may give nothing, which the steps accept as a result. Level Detective and Feed the Village use simplified diets and made-up farm numbers, and say so. Facts a person should check before the unit goes live: the Lindeman details (Cedar Bog Lake, the rejection of the paper at first, Hutchinson's help, his death at 27 in 1942), the human trophic level of about 2.2, the claim that crops store about 1 part in 100 of sunlight, the claim that grazers eat under a fifth of forest leaves, the 1977 and 1981 vent discoveries, the figure for bird and fish growth efficiency, the compost heap at 50 degrees or more, and the three videos, which are still to be chosen.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1942 a paper appeared in the journal Ecology that changed how scientists look at nature. Its author, a young American called Raymond Lindeman, had studied a small lake in Minnesota called Cedar Bog Lake. Before him, a common way to describe a place was to list who lives there and count them. In 1927 Charles Elton had shown a pyramid of numbers, with many small animals and few big ones. Lindeman asked a different question: how much energy goes up from one level to the next? He measured the plants, the grazing animals and the hunters, and the dead matter in the mud, and found that each level held only a fraction of the one below. Reviewers at first refused his paper, saying it had too little data. His teacher, G. Evelyn Hutchinson, argued for it, and it was published. Lindeman died that summer, at the age of 27. It is now one of the most important papers in ecology.
how_we_found_out.who: Raymond Lindeman, with the help of his teacher G. Evelyn Hutchinson
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many ecologists thought the way to understand a lake or a forest was to list and count who lives there. Counting can mislead, because one tree can carry thousands of insects. Lindeman showed that following the energy, and including the dead matter in the mud, tells you much more.

quiz: A green field stores only about one hundredth of the sunlight that falls on it, or less.
Plants catch a very small part of the sunlight, and turn only that part into sugar.
Exactly one tenth of the energy always passes to the next level, like a law of nature.
Measured numbers range from under 2 to over 30 in 100, depending on who is eating.
Every living body gives off heat because cells use food and oxygen to free energy.
This is respiration: food and oxygen make carbon dioxide, water and heat.
A pyramid of energy can be upside down, just like a pyramid of numbers can.
Energy flowing through a level cannot be more than what it got from the level below.
One big tree can feed thousands of insects, so a pyramid of numbers can be upside down.
A few large producers can support many small eaters, so the bottom bar is the narrower one.
Decomposers are the end of the food chain, and nothing eats them.
Nematodes graze on fungi and bacteria, and springtails eat fungi, so decomposers feed others too.
Some food chains in the deep sea begin with chemicals, not sunlight.
Near hot vents in total darkness, bacteria make food from chemicals and animals feed on them.
An animal who eats grass and also insects always sits at level 3.
Her level is the average level of her food plus one, so it can be between 2 and 3.
Atoms in living things are used again and again, but energy is not.
Atoms go round and round, while energy enters as light and leaves as heat.
Eating plants always uses less land than eating animals.
Cows and goats turn grass and straw, which people cannot digest, into food, often on land where crops will not grow.
odd: Cow, goat and rabbit eat producers, so they are at level 2; a hawk eats other animals, at level 3.
Dung beetle, earthworm and fungus feed on dead matter; a hawk hunts living animals.
Atoms are used again and again; heat leaves living things and is not used again.
Sugar, starch and fat hold chemical energy in joined atoms that a body can free; salt holds none to use.
Cold-blooded lizards, frogs and snakes burn little food for heat, so pass on more; a warm-blooded sparrow passes on less.
